source.title: Double Descent: Understanding Linear Model Estimation of Nonidentifiable Parameters and a Model for Overfitting

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own simulation of test prediction error across polynomial linear models of increasing size. This conceptually tests double descent in a different model class and setting from the deep-network claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own polynomial-model simulation results in Tables 1 and 2. Cited results from other work and discussion of neural networks without experiments on them are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own simulation of minimum-norm least-squares polynomial regression over a sequence of growing models (Tables 1–2). Prediction error peaks at the interpolating cubic model and falls for the over-parameterized quartic model. This is a non-deep-network test of the general double-descent curve (V4). The author also argues that the second descent comes from model specification rather than capacity itself.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The author also explicitly argues that double descent is really about under-fitting, and that observing it requires 'dross' (useless) models in the sequence. The over-parameterized fits still have substantial bias from non-identifiable parameters, so predictions 'leave much to be desired'. Fitting an appropriate model matters more than sample size.
record.recipe_differences: The study simulates polynomial linear regression and evaluates mean squared prediction error over a sequence of least-squares models; it does not reproduce a deep-network training or size sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported pattern changes with training sample size: at n = 301 and n = 3001 the cubic model is no longer an interpolation model and is not severely overfitted. The authors also state that different random selections of predictor variables can change the table values substantially, while the overall patterns remain similar.

fits_no_version.finding: The author argues double descent is 'really about under fitting'. On this view the second descent appears only because the model sequence passes through useless terms before reaching a correct specification, and triple descent is possible.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The second descent reflects the order in which basis terms are added (misspecified models preceding a correct one), not over-parameterization per se.

record.peer_reviewed: The American Statistician (a revised version was accepted under the title Linear Model Estimation and Prediction for p > n)
record.problems: The evidence is a simulation in one specified polynomial setting, with test sample size n_f = 101. The authors note that values can change substantially with different random predictor selections. No formal uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported PMSE results from Tables 1 or 2 were left out.

untested.parts: No training-time or epoch axis; closed-form minimum-norm estimates.

Only two sample sizes per setting, with n at or above the cubic threshold. Increasing n moves away from the peak, which V3 also predicts lowers error, so the 'more data can hurt' regime is not probed.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
No label-noise or regularization sweep. Triple descent is only speculated, not tested.
No effective-parameter recount of the curve.
Only one polynomial basis and a six-model sequence. No fine-grained capacity sweep past interpolation.

missing.what: Squared-bias column for each model. For example, M4 Bias² is 6.81 at n = 151 versus 0.0021 at n = 301, showing most over-parameterized error comes from the non-identifiable component.
Eigenvalue concentration of Szz for the quartic model: 86 of 200 eigenvalues give 99% of the total at n = 151, so low effective rank does not hold.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V3 'challenges' label is removed. Raising n from the cubic threshold (n = p) to about 2p moves away from the peak, which V3 also predicts lowers error, so these rows cannot challenge V3. Rows at n = 301 and n = 3001 contain no over-parameterized models, so they serve only as non-interpolating controls for V4. No uncertainty estimates are reported, and the author notes values vary with the random predictor draw.

versions.untested_parts: Deep networks and model-wise error in deep networks.
The sample-size comparison is limited to two training sample sizes and does not sweep sample size around the threshold.
The reported simulation is a particular polynomial linear-model setting, not a survey of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample size.
No sweep of label noise or regularization, and no test for triple or multiple descent.
No test of whether an effective-parameter count turns second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.condition: Interpolating settings (n = 151 with 50 predictors; n = 1501 with 500 predictors), minimum-norm least squares
relationships.reason: PMSE peaks at the interpolating cubic model (82360.71; 109707117) and drops sharply for the over-parameterized quartic model (12.30; 12.3). Both are below the quadratic model's error (r3, r4, r5, r15, r16, r17).
relationships.display_finding: PMSE fell from 82360.71 and 109707117 for interpolating cubic models to 12.30 and 12.3 for quartic models, respectively, also beating quadratic-model error.

tranche.reason: Own polynomial minimum-norm least-squares simulations test the general double-descent question using a different method from deep-network sweeps.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v2 dated September 17, 2025. PMSE measures squared error against the conditional mean, averaged over 1000 response vectors and 101 test cases; polynomial models contain no interactions.

statements.correction: V4 limits_scope for further capacity and model-sequence dependence; Table 1 M4→M5 PMSE 12.30→59.84; Table 2 M4→M5 PMSE 12.3→46.6; both sequences retain a sharp cubic-to-quartic second descent.
statements.problem: The reported quintic ascent is correct, but the challenges label overstates its bearing on V4: renewed post-interpolation improvement remains present.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: M3 at the interpolation threshold, comparing the two training sample sizes in each predictor setting
reader_labels.reason: At the reported threshold, increasing training n is accompanied by lower PMSE: 82360.71 to 483.90 for 50 predictors and 109707117. to 15293 for 500 predictors (r4, r10, r16, r22). This does not establish that more data cannot hurt in other settings.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Quartic model following the cubic model, across the reported predictor counts and training sizes
reader_labels.reason: Prediction error drops sharply from the cubic to quartic model in each setting, including where the cubic model interpolates (r4–r5, r10–r11, r16–r17, r22–r23).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Quintic models and larger training sample settings
reader_labels.reason: PMSE rises again from quartic to quintic in all four settings, and with the larger training sample the cubic model is not an interpolation model; the paper describes the quintic results as overfitting (r6, r12, r18, r24).
